title: I tested ML meta-labeling on my crypto trend bot and it added nothing (AUC 0.52). Is a plain 4h EMA system the better path? Looking for critique
author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
selftext:
How I got here: a few weeks ago I saw a Twitter post with a "prompt to get rich with Claude." I didn't get rich, obviously, but I was surprised by how fast and how well the AI could build and test things with me. So I kept going: \~250 variants backtested, most of them failed, and what's left is the simple system below. Now I want humans to tell me what I'm missing.



Hobbyist here, small account (\~$240, money I can afford to lose). I tried adding machine learning as a filter on my rule-based trend bot (20 features, walk-forward, 3 models). AUC came out at 0.51–0.53 and it didn't beat random filtering, so I'm running the plain rules live. I'd like experienced eyes on the method before I trust it.



**Rules (fixed in advance, not optimized):**



\- 45 altcoin USDT-M perpetuals, 4h candles

\- Entry: EMA 20/50 cross, only in the direction of EMA 200. Limit order 0.05% better than the close, valid 60 min (skipped if not filled)

\- Exit: initial stop 2 ATR(14), trailing stop 3 ATR from the best price, 20-day max

\- Fixed $12.5 per trade (LONG at 64% of that), 3x, max 8 positions per side

https://i.redd.it/anur5xfb9w0i1.png

**Backtest (1h candles, taker 0.05% / maker 0.02% / slippage 0.055% / funding included):**



\- Nov 2020–Nov 2023: 1,285 trades, +$136, t ≈ 3.4, max drawdown $27

\- Nov 2023–Nov 2026: 1,705 trades, +$162, t ≈ 3.6, max drawdown $45

\- \~1/3 winners. The top 10% of winners make more than the total profit

\- 45 of 73 months positive. Worst month −$21.6

\- All 14 neighbor parameter sets (MA lengths, filters, stops, 2h/6h candles) were positive



**Tested and rejected:** BTC regime filters (ADX, trend), funding/OI/taker-ratio filters, fear & greed, ML meta-labeling (AUC 0.51–0.53), Donchian, pairs, grid, DCA, break-even stops, tighter trailing, top-100 universe, shorter timeframes. Most "improvements" just cut trades, so the drawdown went down but the edge didn't change.



**What worries me:**



1. **Selection bias**. The edge shows up in these 45 coins but NOT in other coins of similar age (top-100 universe ≈ 0). I picked the 45 for liquidity, not results, but still.

2. **It's mostly SHORT**. Altcoins bled vs USDT in 2024–25. LONG is around 0. If the regime flips, what then?

3. The last \~9 months are weak.



**Live**: running since Nov 3 with fixed rules. The plan is to judge it at 300 trades (pre-set: stop if average < 0, emergency stop at 100 trades if far worse than backtest). I size up to $18 only after 60 trades with execution matching paper.



**Questions**:



1. How would you test whether the 45-coin edge is real and not selection bias?

2. How do you handle a trend system whose edge depends on one side (SHORT) and one regime?

3. Does continuous sizing by trend strength (Carver style) make sense with such small size and exchange minimums?

4. Anything obviously wrong in how I'm measuring?

5. Has anyone gotten ML to add real value on top of a simple trend signal in crypto? What features or setup made the difference?



Thanks. Happy to share more numbers.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the 0.52 doesn't surprise me. you said the top 10% of winners make more than the whole total, so the system lives on a handful of trades nobody can tell apart from the losers at entry. a filter has to drop trades, and if it drops even two of the big ones it does damage. random filtering matching it is about what I'd expect.

what I'd check before trusting the plain rules is the entry. a limit 0.05% better than the close, good for 60 minutes, only fills when price comes back to you. the moves that run straight away from the cross never fill, and those are the candidates for your top 10%. on 1h candles the backtest can't really tell whether the limit was filled or only touched. run it once with market entries at the next open and see how much of the result is left.

also the 45 coins. if that's today's list applied back to 2020, every alt that died in between is missing, and you can't know which way that moves the result until they're in.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body: Thanks, this is exactly the kind of critique I was hoping for. On the limit entry: I did test market entries at the next open over 3 years (with a second motor that's now off). It stayed positive (t ≈ 2.9 vs 3.8 with the limit), so the edge doesn't seem to depend on the limit. But you're right that 1h candles count "touched" as filled, and my live data already shows it: 82% fill rate live vs 93% in the backtest. I'll rerun with trend only over 6 years at market, and with a stricter fill model on 1m/5m candles. On survivorship: yes, it's today's 45 applied back to 2020. I'll rebuild the universe point-in-time (top 45 by volume each month among all perps that existed then, delisted ones included) and see which way it moves. Will post the results here either way.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 82% live against 93% in the backtest is the number I'd chase. the 11 points that didn't fill aren't random, they're the trades where price never came back, and those are mostly the ones that ran. rerun the backtest counting a fill only when price trades through the limit, and see if it lands near 82.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body: That's exactly the test I'm running now. I added fill thresholds (touch, and price trading through by 0.01 / 0.03 / 0.05%) on 1-minute candles to see which lands near 82%, and for that threshold I compare the signals that didn't fill vs the ones that did, both entered at market. If the unfilled ones are the runners, the limit is costing me the tail. Will post the numbers.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body: Results are in (point-in-time universe with 16 delisted perps, 1-minute fills, 1000 random baskets): - Market entries at next open: +6.1c/trade, t 2.9 over 6 years. The edge doesn't depend on the limit. - Fills: "touch = fill" gives 92% (matches my old 93%). Requiring price to trade through by 0.01/0.03/0.05% gives 91/89/87%. And u/QuanTradin was right: the signals that don't fill at 0.05% would have made +13.8c at market vs +3.9c for the ones that filled. The limit still wins overall (fees and slippage saved on \~88% of trades), but it's close, and at my live 82% it's roughly a wash. - Point-in-time universe: +4.4c, t 1.8. Fails my t ≥ 2 bar. SHORT holds at +12c in both halves. LONG is −2.1c. - 1000 random 45-coin baskets: median +1.7c, 81% positive, 8% with t ≥ 2. My list sits at the 93rd percentile. So there's an edge, smaller than I thought, it's in the short side, and my list was on the lucky end. Next: long at 64% vs 32% vs short-only on the unbiased universe. Thanks both, this changed how I read my own numbers.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body: Follow-up: on the unbiased universe, cutting longs to 32% or short-only doesn't beat 64% in both halves (longs helped in 2020-23, hurt in 2023-26), so I'm keeping 64%. On entries, u/QuanTradin's point held up: "limit, else market after 60 min" was the worst option by far, the runners are gone by then. Moving the limit from 0.05% to 0.02% off the close fills more (87% → 90% with strict fills) and wins in both halves, so that's the only change.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the short side holding at +12c in both halves is the result I'd keep, and I'd stop calling it one system. long at -2.1c on the unbiased universe looks like the half your list was flattering. one caution on the next test: three variants on the same data is three more tries, so hold the t bar a bit higher for whichever wins.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body: Fair on both. I'll treat them as two systems from here: short is the edge, judged on its own at 300 trades. Long stays on at 64% as a regime hedge, but on probation with its own pre-set rule: after 100 long trades (live + paper), if the average is below zero it moves to paper only. And point taken on multiple tries: the 0.02% limit change is within noise, so I'm treating it as a free tweak with a mechanical reason, not a proven improvement. Thanks, this thread was worth more than the last 50 backtests.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good that you fixed the rules in advance and wrote down your stop conditions before going live, that's the part most people skip. For the selection worry, I'd rebuild the 45-coin list using only what was known at each start date, like liquidity back then, and see if the edge survives. Also run the same rules on randomly picked coins from the broader list many times, to see how often a random 45 looks as good. Since it leans on shorts in one regime, I'd test the long and short sides separately and size small until the long side proves itself. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and can hold out the last part of the history, which gives another place to check results.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body: Thanks. The point-in-time universe is the top test on my list now (another commenter raised it too). The random-45 idea is great, I hadn't thought of framing it that way. I'll draw the samples from the full history including delisted perps, so survivorship doesn't sneak back

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
Really well laid out, and the fact that you list what you rejected puts this ahead of most posts here. Some thoughts on your questions:

4 first, because it matters most. You tested \~250 variants. The best of N pure-noise strategies tends to show a t-stat around sqrt(2 × ln N), and for 250 that's about 3.3. Your t of 3.4–3.6 sits right at that line. Also check how t is computed: with up to 8 positions per side open at once, trades in the same week are mostly one bet on "alts drop", so a per-trade t overstates it. Resample by month instead. My guess is it drops below 3.

1. Selection bias. The top-100 result coming out near zero is the most important number in your post. Two checks:  
\- Pick the coin list point-in-time. At each date, take the 45 most liquid coins as of that date, not as of today. Coins that are liquid today are partly selected by how they did.  
\- Run a placebo: many random 45-coin subsets from the same point-in-time universe through the same rules. If your 45 sit in the top few percent, that's selection. If they're mid-pack, the edge is in the rules.

2. The short side. Alts bled against USDT in 2024–25, so random shorts with the same holding times would also have made money there, and shorts collected funding too. Compare your shorts to random short entries with matched holding time and frequency. Only the excess over that counts as edge. If most of it disappears, what you have is mostly a bet on the alt-bleed regime, which is a fine thing to know before sizing up.

3. Continuous sizing with $12.5 per trade and exchange minimums will mostly be rounding noise. I'd keep it fixed until the account is big enough that the size steps are actually small.

On QuanTradin's limit-order point, agree it's worth checking: a limit 0.05% better than the close fills on pullbacks, and the clean runaway moves never fill. If the 1h backtest fills on touch, it's probably taking exactly the big winners that live would miss. Fill only when price trades through, and see what's left.

5. AUC 0.51–0.53 is what I'd expect too. Meta-labeling can't pick out the few big winners at entry if nothing at entry distinguishes them, and your "top 10% make more than the total" says nothing does.

Your live plan with pre-set stop rules is the right move. I'd just add a written note now of what result at 300 trades would count as "matches backtest", so the bar can't move later.

If you're up for going deeper, send me a DM. I'd be happy to run your trade log through the checks above (month resampling, random-short placebo, random coin subsets) and talk through what comes out. No selling, just comparing notes.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body:
Ran your checks. You called it.



\- Monthly resampling (72 months): shorts on the point-in-time universe go from t 3.3 per trade to t 1.8 per month. The 95% interval on monthly P&L includes zero for every version. Not significant.

\- Random-short placebo, same coin/month/side, 200 runs: with the bot's own exits, random shorts make −0.4c vs the bot's +12.0c (p < 0.01), so the entry signal does something. But random shorts held for the same duration without stops make +19.5c, more than the bot. Most of the short P&L is the alt-bleed regime. Longs are indistinguishable from random entries.

\- Point-in-time random 45 from each month's top 100: median +2.1c, 96% positive. The volume-ranked list sits at the 81st percentile. Selection doesn't matter much.

\- Written bar for 300 live trades: expected +4.4c, ±16.9c margin. "Matches" if the mean lands between −12.4 and +21.3c. Confirming +4.4c would take \~4,300 trades.



So: no proven edge. A short book that mostly rides a regime, with an entry signal that beats random. I'll keep it running small as an experiment, move longs to paper, and not size up. Thanks for the push, this saved me from scaling on a t-stat that wasn't real.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Great work, and genuinely rare to see someone run the checks and post the answer straight.

One thing in your numbers I'd look at next. Random shorts with your exits: -0.4c. Random shorts held the same time with no stops: +19.5c. Your bot: +12.0c. So the entry beats random, but in this regime the exits cost more than the entry adds. The 2 ATR stop and trailing are probably cutting shorts that would have worked a few bars later, which is exactly what you'd expect in a slow bleed with noisy bounces. That doesn't mean "remove the stops", since a regime flip is where they save you. But it does tell you the exit logic, not the entry, is where the system loses money right now.

Also interesting that point-in-time random subsets came out 96% positive while your earlier top-100 run was near zero. If that earlier run used today's top-100, survivorship cut the other way there: coins that are still big today are the ones that didn't bleed.

Your written bar is the honest part: ±16.9c at 300 trades means live can't confirm or kill it, only flag a disaster. Keeping it small is the right call.

The DM offer stands if you want to dig into the exit side together.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body:
Ran the exit grid on shorts only, point-in-time universe, 11 variants fixed in advance (stop 2/3/4 ATR x trail 3/4/5, plus time-only 10/20 days), split by month regime (47 alt-down months, 25 not).



Your read holds in down months: looser exits match or slightly beat mine there. But in the 25 non-down months, every looser exit loses more (−9.9 to −15.9/month vs −9.0 for 2/3), and time-only is worst. Over 6 years, 2 ATR stop / 3 ATR trail comes out best on total, drawdown and both halves. So the stops aren't the leak, they're what keeps the non-bleed months survivable.



Cleanest takeaway from the whole thread: the short book makes about +8.8/month when alts fall and loses about −9.0/month when they don't. It's a regime bet with decent exit management, and I'm sizing it like one.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Fair enough, that's a clean answer and it overturns half of my read. The stops are paying for themselves in the months that matter for survival.

One thing I'd add before sizing: the down/not-down split is labeled after the fact. You only know a month was "alt-down" once it's over. So the real question is whether the regime is predictable at the start of the month. If it isn't, your expected value is just the base rate: 47 × 8.8 − 25 × 9.0 ≈ +189 over 72 months, about +2.6/month, and all of it comes from alts having fallen in 65% of months. That's a bet that the base rate holds.

Two checks I'd run on that:  
\- Does last month's regime predict this month's? If down months cluster, there's something to lean on. If it's close to a coin flip, there's nothing to time.  
\- Compare the book to a plain equal-weight short of the same 45 alts at the same average exposure, funding included. If the book doesn't clearly beat the passive short, the entry and exit logic is mostly a more complicated way to hold the same beta.

Either way, "regime bet with decent exit management, sized like one" is the honest description.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body: That's the right framing. Without a way to see the regime coming, the expectancy is just the base rate: \~65% alt-down months, about +2.6/month. I'll run both checks: regime persistence (does a down month predict the next one, vs the 65% base rate), and the book vs an equal-weight passive short of the same point-in-time 45 at matched average exposure, funding included on both sides (my sim had no funding so far). If the book can't beat the passive short month over month, I'll say so here.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Sounds like the right plan. Two small things before you run it:

1. Funding: the original post says "fees, slippage and funding included", but you mention the sim had none so far. Which runs had it? For an alt short book it can go either way: shorts collect funding in normal times, but in crowded-short stretches they pay it, often exactly during squeezes. Worth knowing which numbers in the thread are pre-funding.

2. Regime persistence: with \~71 month-to-month transitions, the test is weak. Comparing P(down | last month down) vs P(down | last month not down), the standard error of the difference is about 12pp, so you'd only reliably detect a gap of roughly 30+ percentage points. A "no persistence" result there won't mean much. A big gap would.

Looking forward to the passive-short comparison, that one should be the most decisive.

replies.author: Repulsive_Cloud_7435
replies.body:
Good catches, both fair:

1. **Funding:** you’re right, and my original post was inaccurate on that point. Labs 13 through 13.4 had no funding. 13.5 is the first in this series that includes it (historical funding for all 354 coins that were ever in the monthly top-45). Result: the bot’s SHORT book *paid* net funding, −12.6 USD over 6 years, taking it from +190 to +178. So it went against us, as you suspected for crowded-short stretches, but small enough that no conclusion changes. Everything earlier in the thread is pre-funding.
2. **Persistence power:** agreed. With \~79 transitions the SE of the difference is \~12pp, so my pre-set 20pp bar was below what the test can resolve. The +2pp result only rules out a *large* persistence effect, not a small one. Practically it doesn’t change anything for me: I wouldn’t build a live regime filter on an effect too small to measure.

The passive-short comparison came out as the decisive one, results above.  
Ran both checks, rules written down before running (Lab 13.5, point-in-time top-45 universe, 6 years, funding now included from data.binance.vision):

**Regime persistence:** P(down month | previous down) = 64% (32/50) vs P(down | previous not down) = 62% (18/29). +2 pts, Fisher p = 0.53. My pre-set bar was ≥20 pts and p < 0.05, so no exploitable persistence. Last month tells you nothing about next month, which matches my earlier failed attempts at a live regime filter.

**Bot SHORT vs passive equal-weight short** (same 45 coins each month, rebalanced monthly, matched average exposure \~51 USD, funding + rebalance costs on both):

* Bot: +178 USD over 6y, +2.47/month, monthly t 1.5, max DD 76
* Passive: −108 USD, −1.50/month, max DD 158
* Difference: +3.97 USD/month, **monthly t 3.0**, bot wins 47/72 months, correlation 0.66

The edge is mostly defensive: in down months the bot only beats passive by \~2.2/month, but in up months it loses −8.9 vs −16.2. The stops are doing the work you suspected they might be costing. Also interesting: a passive alt short lost money even though 63% of months were down, because the up months are that violent. Funding cost the bot −12.6 USD over 6 years, which is negligible.

So my read: the entry/exit logic adds real value over just holding the exposure (t 3.0 survives a √(2 ln N) haircut for the number of things I’ve tried), but the SHORT book on its own is still not significant (t 1.5). It still needs more down months than up months to make money. Not changing anything; the 300-trade bar stands. Thanks, this was the most useful framing so far.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
That's the most useful result in the thread, and a nice one: the logic beats just holding the exposure, and it does it exactly where a passive short dies.

One small correction on the haircut: for \~250 variants, sqrt(2 × ln 250) is about 3.3, so t 3.0 sits right at the noise ceiling rather than clearly above it. The comparison inherits the selection, since the book was picked from those 250 on the same data. I'd read it as "promising, not proven", which is basically where you landed anyway.

The defensive shape also makes sense mechanically: stops turn a short into something closer to a capped-loss bet, and that's worth most when the up months are as violent as yours. The passive short losing money with 63% down months says it all. If you ever want to separate "entry" from "stops", random entries with your exact stops vs passive is the clean version.

300-trade bar unchanged is the right call. Thanks for running everything in public, it's been a great thread.
